title: Anyone else have a sense of urgency to complete their game(s)?
author: Moist_Signal_5080
selftext:
Idk if I’m the only one but it feels like there’s a lot of looming “threats” for AI game dev.  
\-Will it become even more accessible they literally everyone can make a game? Some argue that now, but there’s still a fair amount of friction if you’re not committed.  
\-or will it go the opposite direction? AI becomes less accessible due to price hikes, regulations, restrictions.  
\-someone else will make a game similar to mine before me  
\-I have to squeeze every ounce of usage out of my 5 hour window as possible so my subscription is utilized fully.

Just a few things that keep me thinking..

comments.author: ponderdiggums
comments.body:
1) This isn't a concern for me. Tech literacy boundaries naturally soften with time anyways. What will set games apart is Visuals, Design, Storytelling and QA. It's still painfully obvious when a vibe coding dev lacks the skills/experience in these areas and relies on AI. Even once that threshold is crossed, I'd still prefer doing my own design and storytelling because those are a form of expression for me - I'm not as interested in an AI's simulation of expression as I am a lived experience being conveyed through art. 
2) Given our capitalist framework this is a given, and what most people are worried about. Corporations will have sourced all of this creative content for their corporate tool without royalties or credit, and the general populace will be locked/priced out from this knowledge and accumulation of skill sets. 
3) Eh, good for them. I'm a creative, not a businessman. Suit methodology has poisoned the industry, I don't bring that into the indie space when I can avoid it. 
4) Yeah haha, I think we all suffer from this. There's a notion of efficiency as a skillset that's expressed in AI development. You can create anything, so long as you can afford the credits. I benefit a bit from my day job and the skill sets I develop there + 10 years in the games industry.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: Definitely not profit driven, my games/ideas are too niche for that lol. I’m making games I believe would be fun or interesting, if someone else wants to buy it, that’s a bonus. I barely made my Steam fee back on my first release, and that’s success for me. Finds my next $100 game entry fee. I’m still at a loss when factoring Claude subscription. But again, I look at it as I’m paying that $20 a month to make games I want to see be made. So I’m cool with that, hopefully it can stay this affordable for me.

replies.author: ponderdiggums
replies.body: Hey, my mistake on the bad read with your goal!

replies.author: Onye_Nacho
replies.body:
Personally, if you just want to make games out of the passion, I would not waste my time using Steam at all (at least so long as their stupid Direct fee exists or is directed towards non-commercial games and mods).

That is what Itch and GameJolt are for - the passion.

I also would not bother charging money for my games either (at least not by forcing a price tag; donations are fine); I just make them completely free and available for anyone who cares to play.

comments.author: gravesisme
comments.body: If you squeeze every ounce out of your 5 hour window, won't your weekly usage limit get hit in like 2 days? I ran into this, so now I'm spending more time writing plans and not just doing ad-hoc prompts that feel cool and end up eating into my weekly quota.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: Yeah I bottom out by Tuesday night every week. Part of my “squeeze” strategy is hoping for a bonus reset, which seems like a 50-50 chance every week. If I don’t get it, then I have wed-Saturday evening off.

replies.author: gravesisme
replies.body: Yeah the Codex bonus resets have been so nice...seems like they are doing it almost every few days. Claude bonus resets seem to have only been issued related to fable bungling, so those aren't likely going to continue, but fingers crossed.

comments.author: sheridap
comments.body:
I think that “one shot” games is really a misnomer. It took me six weeks of constant human in the loop to tweak the game art, animations and transitions. End of day craftsmanship still matters, even if you’re not writing any of the code. Just think of yourself as the player advocate and keep tweaking until you’re happy.

Many folks will jump in but few will run the full marathon to get a game “right” ai or not.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: I’m not too concerned with 1 shots, it’s cool but doesn’t seem like a good approach. It’s a nice start point, but you are going to have to refine beyond that if you want a decent game. Basically gives you some foundation to work on, not entirely different that what I’m doing already.

comments.author: Spudly42
comments.body: I feel these exact things for these exact reasons.

comments.author: DrStrangeLaughTV
comments.body: I feel the same a lot of the time for sure. The fact that grounds me is that we are all limited by assets. And that requires actual effort unless you just have a lot of capital to pay modellers or artists. Ai game dev is not a turnkey solution that any layman can adopt.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: Currently I agree. Do you think we’ll hit a point where none of the extra work is necessary? That’s one of my points, if it gets so easy that you can do it yourself without any skills. I’m not far from that, I understand technology a bit, but I’m no programmer or artist. That’s enough to deter people for now, not if it keeps advancing tho.

replies.author: Tenthul
replies.body:
I worry about your same points, but with this, no, not at all. There is WAY too much nuance in any given aspect of any given feature of any given game. It cannot know the direction you intend to go. If you're going deep enough into your features to matter anyway. Trying to one-shot a feature is no different than trying to one shot the whole game. Every single feature is going to need 100+ prompts. There's too much detail in there for anything worth it's salt. Only people with a real vision for their game will ever have a chance. Anybody asking "what do you guys think of xyz game/gameplay" isn't ever going to complete anything. People just following trends won't be competition.

Art will be the big thing though. Which is so funny how everybody is like "AI replacing artists!" and anybody actually in the weeds here knows it's the furthest thing. They about to get positively inundated with requests/contracts, most of whom will not do a good job detailing what they need, nor will they likely ever finish their game, they will suck to work with, but they will still be a paying customer. Actually hooking up art/ui sucks ass.

comments.body: Yet somehow gamedev survived much longer development cycles with all that fears you mentioned. If your game is good then I wouldn’t worry much. If it’s just another neuroslop shit like 99.99% of what being produced - why worry at all?

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: My worst case is I can no longer use it for whatever reason, price, regulations etc. I have a document of 10 games I really want to make. It’ll be a bummer if something happens and I don’t get to complete them all.

replies.author: ponderdiggums
replies.body:
You're probably doing these already, but adding this because I don't think your fears of getting priced out or blocked by some other sort of restriction are unfounded:

If it helps, use this time to also familiarize yourself with workflows in Unity, Unreal, Godot, etc in such a way that you could make manual fixes or additions - there will be times where this is necessary anyways. Indie game development was still very accessible prior to the rise of AI, even if you weren't confident with coding or making your own art. Leverage the co-pilot that can explain these flows to you in real time. 

Also consider using Claude to build tools/scripts that will still be helpful when tokens dry up/we get priced out.

comments.author: Pasta_Rage
comments.body:
Yeah I feel this way about all of my projects too. I think the anxiety and sense of urgency are understandable because all of this is still so new. Even if you have experience in tech, there’s still so much uncertainty around where AI is headed next, how accessible it’ll remain, how this influx of new ideas and projects will affect the creative landscape and economy, and what all of that will mean for the things we’re making now. It could even change the way we think about creative competition and the pressure to be the first person with an idea, especially as it becomes easier for more people to actually execute on those ideas.   
  
AHH! It's all complicated yet exciting

comments.author: Trashy_io
comments.body:
Nah not really worried quality still take time and effort and is what people want to pay for. Making a game has definitely gotten easier but making a good game has not which means less competition in the long run due to market demand for high quality original content, copy cats and low effort projects are not earning the big bucks check out steam starlts. And can often bring more trouble then good. 

The more I learn about game dev the less I even turn to AI for advice on anything. Its honestly pretty shat at everything outside of structured programming. And even then GL if you don't know what you are doing. AI hype is dead imo latest model reales hoax kinda confirms it

comments.author: Keracus
comments.body: You have to remember, primarily AI development is still driven by humans; for now this means there will be a difference between someone that uses their experience, skillset, personal knowledge to make whatever they're building be different. However in the future, maybe minimum 3-5 years, AI will take over and that's when game development will be a race.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: I’d argue the race is now. To get some games in before they hits. Then it’ll be a flood when it hits that point.

replies.author: Keracus
replies.body:
Yes, there is a form of a race but I wanted to highlight that you still have time to differentiate and use critical thinking skills to make your AI developed game much better than the current competition.

AI is like driving a Lamborghini. Learn to use it properly Vs some random brain rot person that vomits their AI slop out because they just fired 2-10 prompts into Fable5/Sol and think they're done lol.

comments.author: ezoterik

I think AI is making game dev more accessible, but it still takes a lot of effort to get a product made. Of course, building a product is only part of the battle. Making something that people like and enjoy is still tough. And then even if it is fun, would they pay for it? 

Obviously people have different goals when developing, but worth being honest where AI is a limitation.

comments.author: Rude_Context_4844
comments.body: Yes sometimes

comments.author: gobble_d_goat
comments.body:
Of course. 

Even as a professional software eng trying to build some passion projects in the gaming space, I can’t help feeling anxiety when I see everything coming out so quickly around me. Especially because I’ve been trying to treat it the way I would professional software - granularly scoped, reviewed, tested, and intentionally designed/documented. 

Sure the newest models r one-shotting fairly polished looking games, but the more I see I also start to notice the similarities between them all. Generally a lack of intentional design choices and actually interesting ideas. 

There are of course some gems though, where an actually novel idea is posted/released, and you can tell even with the noise. But thats nothing new, real creativity has and always will stand out. 

At least thats what I tell myself. Keep at it!

comments.author: gcdhhbcghbv
comments.body: You are part of the “literally everyone can make a game” train, so how about you stop complaining about it.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body:
Nah there’s still friction. We’re at the “you don’t need to know how to code phase”. There’s a lot more work than just coding. I’ve been working on my game for 6 months, and it’s still not complete. I believe there may potentially be a point where the friction is reduced or eliminated. Also we are in the era of “ai is the enemy of game dev”, which also stops people from using it. That may or may not blow over eventually.

Also show me the part where I’m complaining. This is just my racing thoughts dumped here for discussion.
